graphicEarnsIt.says: A sheet of alphabet tiles that is visibly being harvested: in beat 1 six cells are ringed in red, and in beat 2 those exact cells are empty holes. It shows the letters of the title being physically cut out of a specimen sheet, so the picture states the mechanism the words only name. LEFT's frames encode nothing beyond the word itself.

A specimen sheet of every available letter, with the ones the title needs boxed in red in beat 1 and then gone (blank tan slots) in beat 2. It encodes supply and depletion: these specific glyphs were physically cut out of the sheet and pasted into the word above, so the tray shows the source and the cost of building the wordmark. It is the only picture in either cut doing work the type cannot.

A full alphabet specimen sheet acting as the donor for the collage: in the first beat certain cells (A, M, R, S, plus the O) carry red cut-marks, and in the second beat those exact cells are empty holes. The picture shows which glyphs were physically taken out of the sheet and carried up into the word above, so it encodes provenance and the running cost of building the wordmark, letter by letter. The empty squares are a tally of what has been used.

perBeat.why: LEFT is one word floating in an empty landscape frame with two thirds of the canvas dead, while RIGHT pairs the same headline with a letter-specimen tray that fills the lower band and marks the letters about to be used.

RIGHT's tray sits on top of the wordmark and swallows the entire second line, so the payoff reads as 'RANSOM' with a row of cropped shapes under it, whereas LEFT shows RANSOM NOTES complete and legible.
